wines.name: Granbazán Etiqueta Ámbar Albariño
wines.sub: Rías Baixas DO · Val do Salnés, Galicia, Spain
facts: 40+ years; half estate, half local growers
wines.flag: The amber label is the house classic. Etiqueta Ámbar made Granbazán's name in the 1990s and was poured by the glass at El Bulli for years. Vintage not on the email: check the bottle.
factors: Cool, wet maritime. Val do Salnés is the coldest, rainiest and most Atlantic of the Rías Baixas subzones. High rainfall and humidity mean rot risk; acidity stays high.
Vines in the region are traditionally trained on high pergolas (parras), which lift the grapes off the damp ground for airflow and reduce rot.
Free-draining granite and sand, which helps in such a wet climate and gives a stony, saline character.
Albariño: thick skins (resists rot), high acid, aromatic but not overpowering: peach, citrus, flowers, a salty finish.

Destemmed, a few hours of cold skin contact, free-run juice only. Fermented in temperature-controlled steel, then about 8 months on the lees with more stirring (bâtonnage) than Granbazán's other wines. More texture and weight than a basic Albariño.
Winemaker Diego Ríos spent time in the Mosel working with Riesling, which shows in the wine's acid structure.
wines.concl: Very good. High, Riesling-like acidity balanced by ripe stone fruit and lees texture; intense and long for its price.
exam: Rías Baixas subzones: Val do Salnés (coolest, wettest), O Rosal and Condado do Tea (warmer, inland along the Miño).
Pergola training: airflow and rot control in a humid climate.
Lees ageing with bâtonnage adds body and creaminess without oak.
pair: Oysters, clams, pulpo a la gallega
wines.say: The Albariño El Bulli poured by the glass: lime, white peach and sea salt, with extra body from eight months on its lees.

wines.name: Domaine Thibert Les Longeays
wines.flag: Pouilly-Vinzelles is the little neighbour of Pouilly-Fuissé, a tiny Mâconnais village appellation just east of it. Les Longeays is a named vineyard (climat) on the right bank of the Valouse stream. Vintage not on the email: check the bottle.
factors: Moderate continental, but the Mâconnais is the warmest, sunniest part of Burgundy. Riper, rounder Chardonnay than the Côte d'Or or Chablis.
Clay-limestone, well drained. Limestone keeps freshness and a mineral edge.
Chardonnay: neutral and site-expressive; picks up apple, pear and citrus here, with stone fruit in riper years.
Gentle pressing, fermented mainly in temperature-controlled stainless steel, then several months on fine lees. Any oak is discreet, so expect texture rather than toast.
Family estate founded in 1967 in Fuissé, nearly 30 ha, now run by Christophe and Sandrine Thibert.
wines.concl: Very good. Rounded fruit kept lively by precise acidity; lees texture and a saline finish give length and some complexity.
wines.ready: Can drink now, but has potential for ageing (3–5 years, per the producer).
exam: Mâconnais hierarchy: Mâcon → Mâcon-Villages → village AOCs (Pouilly-Fuissé, Pouilly-Vinzelles, Saint-Véran, Viré-Clessé).
Since 2020 Pouilly-Fuissé has Premier Cru vineyards: the Mâconnais's first.
Compare with last week's Rue de Bois: Côte de Beaune Chardonnay in used barrels vs Mâconnais Chardonnay mostly in steel.
wines.say: Sunny southern-Burgundy Chardonnay next door to Pouilly-Fuissé: pear, apple and a salty, mineral finish, with no heavy oak.

wines.name: Domaine du Gros 'Noré Bandol Rosé
wines.flag: Check the vintage for the blend. The 2025 is 50% Mourvèdre, 30% Cinsault, 20% Grenache; the 2019 was 54/25/19 plus 2% Clairette. Alain Pascal is a former boxer who sold his grapes to other estates before bottling his own in 1997.
factors: Warm Mediterranean, but the amphitheatre of slopes faces the sea, and the Mistral and sea breezes cool the vines. Mourvèdre, a very late ripener, needs this heat to ripen.
Clay and limestone terraces around La Cadière d'Azur. Poor, well-drained soils hold yields low (about 30 hl/ha).
Mourvèdre gives structure, savoury herbs and age-worthiness. Cinsault adds freshness and red fruit; Grenache adds body and strawberry.
Recent vintages: Grenache and Cinsault get a short maceration, Mourvèdre is direct-pressed, then blended. Fermented in concrete or steel, no wood, bottled in spring.
wines.concl: Very good. Structured, savoury and long for a rosé; Mourvèdre gives grip and weight that most Provence pinks lack.
wines.ready: Drink now, but has potential for ageing (a few years).
exam: Bandol: red must be at least 50% Mourvèdre with 18 months in oak; rosé and white also made.
Mourvèdre: late-ripening, needs heat; gives tannin, dark fruit and gamey or herbal savouriness in reds.
Most Provence rosé is pale and light; Bandol is the structured, age-worthy exception.
wines.say: Provence rosé with backbone: Mourvèdre-led Bandol, savoury and salty, with blood orange and herbs. It can even age.

wines.name: Les Deux Flèches Moulin-à-Vent
facts: Nicolas & Jérémy, teachers at the Davayé wine school
wines.flag: Not your typical Beaujolais. Mostly destemmed with little or no carbonic maceration, then aged in neutral barrels. Expect a firmer, more Burgundian Gamay than the bubblegum style. The micro-estate began in 2015 with a Fleurie vineyard. Vintage not on the email: check the bottle.
factors: Moderate continental, slightly warmer than the Côte d'Or. Gamay ripens fully here.
Thin topsoil over hard pink granite, rich in manganese and iron. The manganese is said to limit yields and give smaller, thicker-skinned berries: more colour and tannin than other crus.
Gamay: thin-skinned, high acid, low-to-medium tannin, red fruit and floral notes.
Mostly destemmed, native yeasts, fermented in concrete. Little to no carbonic maceration, so fewer banana/bubblegum notes and more structure. Aged up to a year mostly in neutral French oak.
An old-vine parcel: lower yields and more concentration.

ter: earthy / underbrush notes as it ages

wines.concl: Very good. Ripe red fruit, fresh acidity and firm, fine tannins in balance; savoury and mineral notes add complexity.
wines.ready: Can drink now, but has potential for ageing (up to 10 years for top Moulin-à-Vent).
exam: The 10 Beaujolais crus; Moulin-à-Vent is the most structured and age-worthy, and the crus may be sold as Bourgogne.
Carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration give kirsch, banana and bubblegum notes; destemmed fermentation gives more structure.
Compare with last week's Nebbiolo and Hautes-Côtes Pinot: three pale-to-medium reds, three levels of tannin.
wines.say: The most serious Beaujolais cru, made like Burgundy: cherry and rose, with real grip from pink granite.

lineup.sub: An Atlantic Albariño, a Mâconnais Chardonnay, a structured Bandol rosé and a granite-grown Gamay. Vintages weren't in the email, so check each bottle.
rows: Rosé drinkers who want a food wine

blocks.title: Tasting order for a flight
items: The racy Albariño first, then the rounder Chardonnay.
The Bandol has enough body to follow the Chardonnay and bridge into the red.

items: Three rosés now: Cuomo (short maceration, Aglianico), Boudignon (direct press, Cabernet Franc), Gros 'Noré (Mourvèdre, mixed method). Compare colour and body.
